opus-5.5.text:
I think the most interesting part is that the hardest problems were almost never the ones I expected. Coming from research, I assumed the main challenge would be technical: can we train a better model, can we scale efficiently, can we push long context further. Those problems are hard, but they're the kind of hard I'm comfortable with. You can reason about them, run experiments, and get feedback.

What surprised me is how much of starting a company is about things that don't have a clean loss function. How do you build an organization where very talented, very opinionated people can work together and move fast? How do you make decisions when the information is incomplete and the landscape changes every few months? In research you can wait until you're confident. In a company, waiting is itself a decision, and often an expensive one.

Another unexpected difficulty is that you're constantly balancing two timescales. On one side there's the long-term belief: we think AGI is a historic opportunity, and we want to bet on the fundamental capability of models. On the other side there are very short-term pressures: products, users, competitors, fundraising, compute. Many days you feel pulled between them. What I find interesting is that the answer is usually not to choose one, but to find a path where the short-term work actually compounds into the long-term goal. When you find that alignment, things get much easier. When you don't, you feel friction everywhere.

And I'd say there's a personal dimension too. As a researcher you mostly have to be honest with yourself about whether an idea works. As a founder you have to do that at a much larger scale: admit when a direction isn't working, change course, and still keep the team's confidence. That kind of honesty is uncomfortable, but I've come to think it's one of the most important things. The difficulties keep coming, so the real question is whether your process for dealing with them gets better over time.

r001.rationale: The response says the hardest problems were often unexpected and contrasts assumed technical challenges with organizational and business challenges. It does not clearly distinguish expecting difficulties in general from not knowing which specific difficulties will arise.

r002.rationale: The response describes technical problems as hard but approachable through reasoning, experiments, and feedback. It does not say that the solutions to newly arising technical problems cannot be known in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the most interesting thing has been how the hard problems kept shifting under us. Before starting out, I thought the hardest part would be the technology itself—getting the model to work, scaling it up, pushing the capability frontier. Those are real difficulties, but they turned out to be the kind of difficulties you can plan for. You know roughly what the problem looks like, you have some sense of how to attack it.

What surprised me were the problems that don't have a clean shape. For example, how do you keep a team organized around a mission when the whole field is moving so fast that what counted as a breakthrough six months ago is now table stakes? At a university lab you can afford to go deep on one question for years. In a company you have to decide every week what to stop doing, and that's much harder than deciding what to start. Every time you cut something, you're also cutting someone's sense of what they were here to build.

The other thing I found genuinely fascinating is the gap between what you believe about the technology and what you can actually act on. I've had a fairly stable conviction for a long time about where things are heading—that scaling is the main lever, that the models will keep getting more general. But believing that doesn't tell you what to do on a Tuesday when compute is constrained, a key hire falls through, and a competitor ships something you were about to ship. The long-term view and the short-term execution are almost two different skills, and the difficulty is holding both at once without letting one hollow out the other.

And maybe the most unexpected part: I used to think difficulty was something you overcame and then moved past. Now I think of it more as the medium you work in. The interesting problems don't get solved so much as they get replaced by better problems. If you're not hitting unexpected difficulty, it usually means you're not moving fast enough or you're not aiming high enough. So I've come to treat it as a signal rather than a setback—which doesn't make it less painful, but it does make it more interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says the technical difficulties were expected and plannable, while the shifting team and execution problems surprised the speaker, distinguishing general expectations from the specific difficulties that arose.

r002.rationale: It says technical problems had a recognizable shape and a rough approach, and discusses uncertainty in execution, but does not state that the solutions to newly arising technical problems cannot be known in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the most interesting part is how often the problem changes as you work on it. You might start with something that looks like a technical challenge, but then realize the real question is whether you’re building the right thing—or whether the team has the same understanding of what matters.

That requires a different mindset from solving a well-defined research problem. You have to make decisions with incomplete information, learn from what happens, and be willing to revise your assumptions. The difficult part is knowing when to persist and when to change direction. You need conviction to keep going, but you also need to leave room for evidence that you’re wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most interesting part is how the nature of the problems changes as you go. You might start with a technical question, but then discover that the harder question is how to get people aligned on what to build and how to judge whether it’s working.

With a technical problem, you can usually run an experiment and get some evidence. In a company, you often have to make a decision before the evidence is clear. Do we keep exploring, or do we commit? Is something fundamentally wrong, or does it just need more time? You have to act while staying willing to revise your assumptions. That tension is something I find really interesting.
